blogs.title: Same Gun, Different Night: The Intrinsic Evidence Doctrine and Rule 404(b) in Felon-in-Possession Cases
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's holding that testimony about a defendant's prior possession of the same firearm used in the charged offense constitutes intrinsic evidence rather than 404(b) propensity evidence. It examines the doctrinal boundary between intrinsic and extrinsic evidence under Rule 404(b), the 'same weapon' exception recognized in United States v. Battle, and the implications for defendants who possess firearms over extended periods. The post also considers how the intrinsic evidence label effectively circumvents the balancing test of Rule 403 and the notice requirements of Rule 404(b), and whether courts should more carefully scrutinize such characterizations when prior possession is temporally distant from the charged offense.

blogs.title: Deferred Limiting Instructions and the Confrontation Clause: When Is 'Later' Good Enough?
blogs.description: This post examines the district court's decision to deny a pretrial request for an immediate limiting instruction on out-of-court statements, and the Eighth Circuit's approval of deferring such instructions to the close of trial under United States v. Bennett. It analyzes the tension between the Confrontation Clause's guarantees and the practical sequencing of evidence at trial, particularly when police officers testify about victim statements before the victim takes the stand. The post explores whether the Eighth Circuit's reasoning—that the Confrontation Clause is satisfied so long as the declarant ultimately testifies—adequately protects defendants from the risk that jurors will treat preliminary hearsay as substantive evidence before the declarant is available for cross-examination.

blogs.title: Reading Police Reports During Cross-Examination: Authentication Requirements for Impeachment by Prior Inconsistent Statement
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's affirmance of the district court's requirement that defense counsel authenticate a police report before reading portions of it into the record during cross-examination, even when using it to impeach a witness by prior inconsistent statement. It examines the authentication requirement under United States v. Cumbie and the distinction between questioning a witness about prior statements to law enforcement and introducing the resulting report itself as extrinsic evidence. The post also notes the panel's pointed criticism of the government for unnecessarily expanding the issues on appeal—a reminder that appellees should resist the temptation to address arguments the appellant did not pursue—and discusses best practices for defense counsel seeking to use law enforcement reports for impeachment.

blogs.title: When Guidelines Enhancements Clash with the Parsimony Principle: The § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Problem in Armed Career Criminal Cases
blogs.description: This post examines Cutbank's novel argument that the four-level sentencing enhancement under USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) for possessing a firearm in connection with another felony offense produced a within-guidelines sentence that conflicts with 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)'s mandate that sentences be 'sufficient, but not greater than necessary.' It analyzes the complex interaction between the Armed Career Criminal Act's enhanced penalties, the Armed Career Criminal Guideline under § 4B1.4, and the § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement, including the rule that the greater offense level governs. The post explores the broader question of whether stacked sentencing enhancements that produce advisory ranges far exceeding what the ACCA alone would require can ever create a tension with the parsimony principle, and why the Eighth Circuit's presumption of reasonableness for within-range sentences makes this argument exceedingly difficult to win.
